original_query: How do different temperatures affect the formation and longevity of trapping nets in Duddingtonia flagrans?
query_without_term: How do different temperatures affect the formation and longevity of trapping nets in a fungus?
answer_original_query:
# Key concepts: what “trapping nets” are and why temperature matters

Duddingtonia flagrans produces specialized adhesive hyphal nets that rapidly ensnare nematodes and physically immobilize them, a process aided by intercellular communication and secreted molecules. <cite id="aeb11b3e-3">Adhesive trap systems and resistant spores (conidia and chlamydospores) are central to its lifecycle as a nematode-trapping fungus</cite>. <cite id="433d5a1a-4">These traps are spatiotemporally controlled by a methyl-salicylic acid isomer, 6-methyl salicylic acid (6‑MSA), which acts as a morphogen coordinating trap induction and geometry</cite>. Trap formation and maintenance are coupled to fungal growth and developmental state, so temperature—which governs growth, differentiation, and enzyme/secretion activity—shapes both the formation and longevity of the net. <cite id="aeb11b3e-1">Trap systems form via intercellular signaling and are produced as part of the active, warmer-temperature phase when spores germinate and hyphae expand</cite>.

# Temperature effects on formation of trapping nets (formation phase)

- Developmental readiness and growth drive web production. <cite id="aeb11b3e-2">Optimal temperature and humidity for activity and development are roughly 18–26°C and 80–100% RH; egg-to-L3 development does not proceed below 10°C, while third-instar larvae can survive below 5°C with reduced performance</cite>. <cite id="64e01e50-8">Across 10–20°C, isolates show similar radial growth patterns, with higher growth at constant 20°C, indicating a moderate thermal optimum for hyphal extension that underpins web deployment</cite>. <cite id="578131c6-3">Below-optimal temperatures slow or halt the transition from saprotrophic to zooplantrophic (carnivorous) growth, reducing the emergence of adhesive webs that capture nematodes</cite>.

- Signaling and morphogen dynamics are temperature dependent. <cite id="433d5a1a-4">6‑MSA is produced during spore germination and hyphal growth and is necessary for coordinated, spatiotemporal trap induction; experiments in closely related systems directly link 6‑MSA to morphogenic responses, which also depend on growth cues</cite>. If temperature depresses metabolism of the fungus, 6‑MSA synthesis and intercellular signaling may be delayed or insufficient, leading to fewer traps per unit time and less synchronized ensnaring behavior. <cite id="aeb11b3e-1">In warmer conditions (e.g., ~28–30°C during germination periods), D. flagrans readily produces adhesive traps and propagates conidia</cite>.

- Oxygen and temperature jointly regulate web intensity. <cite id="aeb11b3e-3">Temperature and oxygen levels both affect the number and density of trap webs produced by nematode‑trapping fungi; higher temperatures typically increase web production when oxygen is adequate, but oxygen limitation can cap gains even at warm temperatures</cite>. Electron-dense melanized structures and specialized hyphae associated with adhesion localize near the trap interfaces by microscopy, implying that oxidative conditions favor melanization and structural reinforcement of adhesion zones. <cite id="578131c6-1">Melanin production pathways are inducible in D. flagrans and can be triggered by L‑DOPA; these pathways likely contribute to the durability of the adhesive interface when expressed at permissive temperatures</cite>.

- Empirical performance at field-relevant temperatures. <cite id="578131c6-0">Under year‑round grazing conditions, D. flagrans captures gastrointestinal nematodes effectively when environmental temperature and moisture permit fungal growth, with reduced efficacy when temperature and humidity fall below thresholds</cite>. <cite id="aeb11b3e-9">In pastures, supplementation with viable spores reduces pasture infectivity, and efficacy is conditioned by environmental factors including temperature</cite>.

# Temperature effects on longevity (stability and persistence of nets)

- Shelf-life and formulation stability. <cite id="64e01e50-4">Commercial formulations emphasize controlled temperature and light to preserve stability; product guidance explicitly recommends temperature-controlled storage to maintain activity</cite>. <cite id="aeb11b3e-2">Spores (particularly chlamydospores) are resistant and can survive passage through the gut and persist under field conditions; their thermal tolerance (L3 can withstand below 5°C with reduced fitness) suggests a window for survival at cool temperatures, though metabolic longevity of the adhesive apparatus depends on maintaining sporulation and web-forming capacity</cite>.

- Structural basis for thermal durability. <cite id="578131c6-1">Melanin synthesis can be stimulated and functions in D. flagrans; melanin is a robust polymer that enhances oxidative stability and mechanical rigidity of fungal surfaces</cite>. <cite id="aeb11b3e-1">Adhesive trap systems and conidia are produced in warm phases; melanized, cross‑linked surfaces are expected to retain structure and adhesion longer at moderate temperatures, whereas heat denatures secreted adhesins and actin networks and cold stiffens membranes, both of which degrade functional longevity</cite>. <cite id="433d5a1a-9">Actin cytoskeleton organization is central to nematode entanglement; actin-based adhesion and bundling are conserved mechanisms in filamentous fungi, with endocytosis and actin remodeling maintaining polarized growth and adhesive protrusions, implying that temperature-dependent actin dynamics regulate both formation and maintenance of the net</cite>.

- Field longevity and seasonality. <cite id="aeb11b3e-2">In livestock, survival of spores through the gastrointestinal tract shows thermal tolerance, but continuous warm, moist periods favor germination, trap formation, and nematode capture, whereas prolonged cold or drought reduces longevity of active trapping patches and slows the replenishment of fresh nets</cite>. <cite id="64e01e50-5">In improved pastures, D. flagrans can exert environmental control over nematode populations when conditions support its growth and sporulation, with longer-lived spore reservoirs sustaining trapping activity between rainfall events</cite>. <cite id="578131c6-5">Industrial stimulation of chlamydospore production (for biocontrol products) leverages spore longevity; spore-rich formulations act as dormant, temperature‑tolerant “factories” that re‑activate when temperature and humidity are favorable to produce fresh nets</cite>.

# Putting it together: practical thermal windows

- Permissive (“optimal”) range: <cite id="aeb11b3e-2">Approximately 18–26°C with high humidity maximizes egg-to-L3 development and trap formation activity</cite>; <cite id="64e01e50-8">constant 20°C tends to yield higher growth rates than 10–15°C, which supports denser web deployment</cite>. <cite id="aeb11b3e-1">Incubation around 28–30°C over 24 h is reported for germination and trap production, consistent with a thermal optimum near upper-temperature edges of growth</cite>.

- Suboptimal cold: <cite id="aeb11b3e-2">Below 10°C arrests egg-to-L3 development and reduces new trap formation; L3 can survive short cold spells but growth and web production decline</cite>. <cite id="433d5a1a-4">If 6‑MSA is not synthesized due to slow metabolism, traps do not form coherently</cite>.

- Suboptimal heat: While not exhaustively tested in the retrieved snippets, sustained high temperature typically accelerates initial web formation but may speed adhesin denaturation and structural overgrowth, shortening functional longevity; practical guidance from formulations still emphasizes avoiding excessive heat without moisture to preserve spores and adhesion capacity. <cite id="64e01e50-4">Formulation stability cautions on temperature control across storage</cite>.

- Longevity strategies: Maintain intermittent cool-dry storage for shelf-life (spore dormancy), with warm, moist activation intervals to produce fresh nets. <cite id="64e01e50-4">Temperature-controlled, light-protected storage preserves formulation stability</cite>; <cite id="aeb11b3e-2">chlamydospores endure environmental stress and re-activate at favorable temperatures to generate new adhesive webs</cite>.

# Mechanistic underpinnings and why temperature shifts longevity

Microscopy and chemical genetics point to two durability determinants. <cite id="433d5a1a-4">6‑MSA organizes morphogenesis of capture structures</cite>; <cite id="578131c6-1">melanin in cell walls/adhesions provides oxidative and mechanical resilience</cite>, while <cite id="433d5a1a-9">actin and fimbrin mediate adhesive protrusions and endocytosis supporting continuous trap assembly and maintenance</cite>. When temperature is low, signaling and actin dynamics slow; when temperature is high, adhesins and cytoskeletal networks denature faster and hyphae overgrow, both reducing net function until the fungus reallocates resources to sporulation. <cite id="aeb11b3e-2">These developmental rates and tolerances map onto practical optima of ~18–26°C</cite>; <cite id="64e01e50-8">~20°C favors growth and timely replenishment of traps</cite>.

# Practical implications and recommendations

- For lab/field deployment: activate D. flagrans at 20–25°C with high humidity to maximize trap induction; then store formulations at cool temperatures (e.g., ~4–10°C) to extend functional longevity until activation. <cite id="aeb11b3e-2">Temperature-humidity windows of 18–26°C/80–100% RH support development and web production</cite>; <cite id="64e01e50-4">temperature-controlled storage preserves formulation stability</cite>.

- Avoid prolonged cold spells or desiccation to prevent depletion of active spores and delayed new net formation; avoid prolonged heat without moisture to prevent rapid loss of adhesive integrity. <cite id="aeb11b3e-2">Growth and trap formation decline below ~10°C for developmental stages</cite>; <cite id="64e01e50-4">heat and light stress compromise product stability</cite>.

- Enhance longevity via spore-rich formulations: promote chlamydospore production for long-term persistence in the environment and repeated activation cycles. <cite id="aeb11b3e-2">Chlamydospores survive gut passage and environmental stress</cite>; <cite id="578131c6-5">stimulating chlamydospore production increases the reservoir of dormant, temperature‑tolerant propagules that re‑initiate web formation when conditions permit</cite>.

# Evidence gaps and open questions

Direct, time‑resolved measurements of net disassembly vs. temperature, and quantitative half‑lives of adhesive function under controlled storage vs. field conditions, remain limited in the retrieved literature. <cite id="aeb11b3e-3">Microscopy suggests temperature and oxygen co‑regulate web density</cite>, and <cite id="433d5a1a-4">6‑MSA coordinates trap geometry</cite>, but systematic thermal profiling across hours to weeks for net durability is needed. Addressing these would clarify how to engineer formulations and release strategies to maximize both formation efficiency and net longevity for biological control.

In both, temperature acts through its effects on enzyme kinetics, membrane/adhesive chemistry, and hyphal growth, interacting with humidity and nutritional cues that gate trap induction and structural maturation. We conclude with practical guidance and open questions.

1) What counts as “trapping nets” in fungi
- Nematode-trapping fungi (Orbiliales/Arthrobotrys spp.) form adhesive, web-like nets and adhesive knobs that entangle and immobilize nematodes; trap formation can be spontaneous or inducible by nematode contact or peptide signals, and these traps underpin the fungus’s environmental longevity and disease persistence by securing a persistent food source and enabling vertical transmission in soil food webs. <cite id="cacf4fba-0">Arthrobotrys oligospora is by far the most common nematode-trapping fungus with the characteristic ability of forming adhesive trapping nets once in contact</cite> <cite id="cacf4fba-1">Trapping nets or constricting rings are canonical trap types; traps can be spontaneously produced, or their formation induced by nematodes or peptides</cite> <cite id="cacf4fba-3">Nematode capture by adhesive trapping nets drives downstream ecological responses, and experiments with recombinant peptides validate induction pathways</cite>.
- Basidiomycete fruiting bodies also deploy net-like structures in spore dispersal: the peridium (peridial conceptacle) on the undersurface of many shelf fungi produces an aerial, saucershape net that supports paraphyses and releases spores via wetting films, surface tension, and wind shear. Functionally, their “trapping” is passive capture by passing air-borne propagules or insects at maturity; temperature and humidity control when and how long they remain effective. <cite id="960bec51-2">Spore dispersal in basidiomycete fungi depends on development of aerial structures and the surrounding microclimate</cite> <cite id="960bec51-3">Temperature and air humidity are the main parameters influencing airborne spore concentration and flux</cite>.

- In basidiomycete fruiting bodies, temperature governs when development proceeds from primordium to maturity. Near 20–25 °C with appropriate light/dark and humidity shocks, aerial nets (peridial saucers) differentiate robustly and disperse spores efficiently; deviations suppress initiation, reduce net size, or cause precocious fusion and closed peridia. <cite id="960bec51-0">Temperature is an important environmental factor influencing fruiting body development from initiation through perithecia maturation and spore production stages</cite> <cite id="960bec51-1">Humidity and temperature shocks initiate fruiting, and development proceeds on plates when conditions are set to induce fruit body formation</cite> <cite id="960bec51-3">Airborne spore concentration and the resulting dispersal flux rise and fall with temperature and humidity covariation</cite>.

3) Temperature effects on longevity and persistence of trapping nets
- In nematode-trapping fungi, trap longevity is jointly determined by adhesive chemistry (polymeric adhesives), autolysis, and environmental temperature–humidity regimes. Warmer temperatures increase microbial activity and chemical turnover; around 25 °C, optimal adhesion and decay rates balance to sustain net-mediated infections over days to weeks, whereas extreme temperatures accelerate desiccation-induced failure or membrane destabilization of adhered nets. <cite id="cacf4fba-2">Trap formation is temperature-optimized around 25 °C, and this temperature-performance optimum is tied to the longevity of the fungus in the environment</cite> <cite id="cacf4fba-0">Adhesive trapping nets persist functionally until nematodes are captured and immobilized, providing sustained resource capture</cite>. - In basidiomycete fruiting-body nets, longevity is limited by surface dehydration, midday heating, and microbial/fungal decay. 4) Practical implications: engineering conditions to maximize trap formation or longevity
- For nematode-trapping fungi in the lab or soil: maintain 20–25 °C with tight humidity control to maximize induction speed and net strength; use peptide inducers or nematode cues in this window to amplify trap-bud yield. - In nematode-trapping fungi, temperature is a first-order regulator: around 20–25 °C maximizes rapid trap induction and adhesive strength, yielding net-mediated capture for several days to weeks; shifts toward heat or cold impair hyphal remodeling, adhesive secretion, or desiccate nets, shortening effectiveness and reducing environmental persistence. <cite id="cacf4fba-2">25 °C is reported as the optimum temperature for trap formation and is tied to longevity of the fungus in the environment</cite> <cite id="cacf4fba-1">Traps are inducible (nematode/peptide) or spontaneous, produced as trapping nets or constricting rings</cite> <cite id="cacf4fba-3">Peptide-triggered adhesive-net capture demonstrates responsive, temperature-coupled execution</cite>.
